podcast.body: Inspired by prostitutes in a Paris alley and a poster for "Serenot D'Burgerec," Sting wrote this song about falling in love with a lady of the night, originally as a jazz-tinged bossa nova. Stuart Copeland's suggestion to stress the second beat on the bass transformed its rhythm into a tango-reggae blend, which was vital to its sound. Despite Sting's initial sheepishness about its "lorid subject matter" and "lurching rhythm," Miles Copeland recognized it as "a god damn classic," leading to the band's signing with A&M Records. The BBC initially banned it for sexual content, but it cracked the American Top 40 in April 1979, peaking at number 32, and later reached number 12 in the UK after re-release. "Roxanne would be the lead single of the police's 1978 debut album Outlandos de Moore, comically bastardized French for Outlaws of Love."

podcast.body: Released in 1978, this signature song, despite not charting in the United States until 1982, ultimately provided The Police with their breakthrough, earning accolades such as induction into the Grammy Hall of Fame and recognition by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame for its blend of reggae, punk, and rock, characterized by Stewart Copeland's distinctive reggae drum pattern. "Roxanne, released in 1978 and did not chart in the United States until 1982, but it was the song that gave the police their big break."
